text: In this way, Dupin said, the boy could match his own mind with his opponents mind and guess what the other would do. <break time="0.8s" /> The Prefect, however, never considered the mind of the man he was hunting, searching only the places where he himself would have hidden it. <break time="0.8s" /> So fixed was he on his own ideas of cleverness that he never imagined a hiding place outside the usual ones. <break time="0.8s" /> The Minister, on the other hand, was both a poet and a mathematician, which meant that he could reason as well as imagine. <break time="0.8s" /> Knowing that the police would search his house, he had stayed away at night on purpose, so that they could search it freely. <break time="0.8s" /> He wanted them to believe that the letter was not in the house, so he would naturally choose a simple hiding place. <break time="0.8s" /> Dupin then mentioned a puzzle game in which one player names a word on a map, and the other must find it. <break time="0.8s" /> Beginners choose names in the smallest letters, but experts choose words in large letters that stretch across the whole map. <break time="0.8s" /> Such words, being too plain, escape the eye, and Dupin became sure that the Minister had hidden the letter by not hiding it at all.
